stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the spring-fed pond?
stimulus: During a 2021 drought, ecologists tracked brook trout in twelve beaver ponds in a Montana watershed. In eleven of them, the shallow water warmed past what trout can tolerate, and most of the fish died. The twelfth pond is fed by an underground spring. It stayed cool, and its trout survived. However, that spring water carries little dissolved oxygen. When winter ice sealed the ponds off from the air, only the spring-fed pond suffered a mass trout die-off. The researchers note that the other ponds were spared largely because the drought had already left them with few trout to lose.
choices: Like most of the ponds in the survey, it lost much of its trout population when the drought warmed its water.
The water source that kept its trout alive through the drought also contributed to their deaths the following winter.
Its spring kept it cool during the drought, which caused it to freeze over earlier than the other ponds that winter.
Over the full year, it lost more trout than any of the other ponds that the ecologists surveyed in the watershed.
explanation: Gather every sentence about the spring-fed pond and put them together. The spring kept the pond cool, so its trout survived the drought. The same spring water is low in oxygen, and once ice cut the pond off from the air, its trout died off. One feature, the spring, both protected the fish and later exposed them. That is what B says, and it claims nothing the text doesn't support.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. The other eleven ponds lost their trout in the drought. The spring-fed pond is the one whose trout survived it.

C.why: You spotted that the spring both helped and hurt, then finished the thought with the wrong cause. The first half is right. But the text never says the pond froze earlier. The winter problem was low oxygen once the ice sealed off every pond, not the timing of the freeze. Read every choice to the end.

D.why: The last sentence says the other ponds had few trout left, and you turned that into a ranking. The text gives no counts, so you can't say which pond lost the most fish over the year.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes spinach in the study?
stimulus: In a study of six leafy vegetables, nutrition researchers measured two things: how much calcium each vegetable contained, and what fraction of that calcium participants' bodies absorbed. For five of the vegetables, the fraction absorbed varied little, so the ones richest in calcium delivered the most usable calcium. Spinach did not fit this pattern. It contained more calcium than any other vegetable tested, yet participants absorbed a far smaller fraction of it. The researchers attribute this to oxalate, a compound in spinach that binds calcium in the gut.
choices: As with the other vegetables tested, its calcium content was a dependable guide to how much usable calcium it delivered.
It contained the most calcium of the vegetables tested, but oxalate reduced how much calcium its leaves actually held.
Unlike the other vegetables tested, its calcium content was not a dependable guide to how much usable calcium it delivered.
It delivered less usable calcium than any other vegetable tested, even though it contained the most calcium of all.
explanation: For the other five vegetables, the absorbed fraction barely changed, so calcium content alone told you which ones gave the most usable calcium. Spinach broke that link. Its content was the highest, but its absorbed fraction was much lower, so its content no longer predicts what the body gets. C states exactly that. It doesn't go further and claim how much usable calcium spinach gave compared with the others, which the text never says.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Content predicted usable calcium for the other five vegetables. The text says spinach 'did not fit this pattern.'

B.why: You put oxalate in the wrong place. The text says oxalate binds calcium in the gut, which lowers absorption. It doesn't lower the calcium in the leaves. In fact, spinach had the highest calcium content of the six.

D.why: You saw that spinach's absorbed fraction was low and treated that as a low total. Usable calcium depends on both the content and the fraction absorbed. Spinach had the most calcium, and the text gives no numbers, so you can't say it delivered less usable calcium than every other vegetable.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Drosera tardiva?
stimulus: In the peat bogs of the Halvard Plateau, nearly all sundews flower in midsummer, once their sticky leaves have trapped enough insects that year to pay for seed production. Ecologist Mireille Aston found that one species, Drosera tardiva, flowers in early spring, before its leaves have even unfolded. Yet its seed counts match those of its neighbors. Aston concluded that its flowers are funded by nutrients the plant stored during the previous summer's hunting.
choices: It relies less on trapped insects than the other sundews of the plateau do.
It flowers earlier than its neighbors and therefore produces fewer seeds.
It pays for its flowers with insects captured before the year it blooms.
It traps the insects that fund its seeds in early spring, before midsummer.
explanation: Put two sentences together. D. tardiva flowers before its leaves unfold, so it cannot have caught any insects yet that year. Aston says its flowers are funded by nutrients stored during the previous summer's hunting. So the insects that pay for its flowers were caught in an earlier year.

A.why: You saw that it doesn't use this year's insects and decided it needs insects less. The text says only that it uses insects from an earlier year. It never says it depends on them any less than the other sundews do.

B.why: The first half is right and the second half is wrong. The text says its seed counts match those of its neighbors, so it does not produce fewer seeds.

D.why: You described the group's habit, catching insects in the year of flowering, and gave it to the exception. In early spring its leaves haven't unfolded, so it can't be trapping insects then.

stem: Based on the text, what do Renn and Owusu indicate about Kessler County?
stimulus: In a study of 40 regional labor markets, economists Tobias Renn and Ama Owusu found that a rise in the minimum wage was followed, in almost every market, by a drop in the hours offered to teenage workers. The exception was Kessler County, where teenage hours rose. However, Kessler's wage increase coincided with the opening of a distribution center that hired heavily from all age groups, and teenage hours there rose by less than adult hours did. The researchers therefore treat Kessler as a market where the expected effect was likely masked.
choices: It shows that a minimum wage increase need not reduce teenage hours.
Its rise in teenage hours probably fits, rather than defies, the wider pattern.
Its wage increase cut teenage hours more sharply than in the other markets.
Its teenage hours rose because the new distribution center hired mostly teenagers.
explanation: The researchers call the expected effect 'masked'. That means they think it was still there, just hidden by the hiring boom. Teenage hours rising by less than adult hours supports this. So the researchers read Kessler as consistent with the pattern, not as an exception to it.

A.why: This is the face-value reading of 'teenage hours rose'. The researchers reject it. The 'However' sentence and the word 'masked' tell you they don't treat Kessler as counterevidence.

C.why: You correctly saw that the effect was probably present, then took it further. The text never compares the size of Kessler's hidden effect with the effect in the other markets.

D.why: The center hired heavily from all age groups, not mostly teenagers. Teenage hours also rose by less than adult hours, which points the other way.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the marsh warbler?
stimulus: Most songbirds that breed in the Varn Valley migrate south along the river each autumn, and the few that break from the group do so in timing, leaving weeks earlier or later than the rest. The marsh warbler breaks from the group in another way. Tracking by ornithologist Lena Fosse showed that it leaves in the same week as its neighbors but first flies east over the mountains before turning south, a detour that adds nearly 900 kilometers but crosses feeding grounds the river route lacks.
choices: It is among the few valley migrants that depart at an unusual time of year.
It departs when most valley migrants do but follows a different route south.
It takes a longer route that brings it to its wintering grounds sooner.
It follows the river south before turning east toward richer feeding grounds.
explanation: The warbler is an exception 'in another way', not in timing. It leaves in the same week as its neighbors. What differs is its route: east over the mountains instead of south along the river. So it matches the group on timing and breaks from it on route.

A.why: You put the exception in the wrong category. The other exceptions differ in timing. The warbler differs in route and leaves in the same week as its neighbors.

C.why: The detour is longer and crosses feeding grounds. The text never says the warbler arrives sooner. That claim sounds reasonable, but nothing in the text supports it.

D.why: This reverses the order. The warbler flies east first and turns south afterward. It does not follow the river at all.

stem: Based on the text, what is true about the groundwater around the Orlen Viaduct's piles?
stimulus: When the Orlen Viaduct was built in 1911, its engineers set its piers on timber piles driven into waterlogged clay, a common practice because wood that stays submerged resists rot. For a century the piles held. However, a drainage project in 2009 lowered the water table along the river by nearly two meters. Inspectors now report that the upper portions of the piles have begun to decay, while the deeper portions remain sound.
choices: It once preserved the piles entirely but now leaves their upper parts exposed to rot.
Its drop in 2009 has caused the piles to decay along their entire length.
It was lowered in 2009 to protect the viaduct from flooding along the river.
It had been slowly weakening the piles for a century before the drainage project.
explanation: Submerged wood resists rot, and for a century the piles held, so the groundwater kept them preserved. Once the water table dropped, only the upper portions began to decay. The same water that protected the piles now leaves their upper parts exposed.

B.why: You saw that the drop caused decay and applied it to the whole pile. The text says the deeper portions remain sound.

C.why: The text never gives a reason for the drainage project. Flood protection is an invented purpose that only sounds plausible.

D.why: The text says the piles held for a century and that submerged wood resists rot. The groundwater protected the piles before 2009. It did not weaken them.

stem: Based on the text, what does Petrosyan indicate about the black-burnished ware?
stimulus: At the Tavush cemetery, archaeologists have recovered more than 300 vessels of a thin, black-burnished ware. None has turned up in the settlement two kilometers away, though excavators there have catalogued tens of thousands of shards of ordinary cooking and storage pots. Chemical tests show that the black vessels were made from the same riverbank clay as those pots, yet residue analysis found no trace of food or oil in any of them. Team leader Sona Petrosyan argues that the ware was likely made for burial rather than borrowed from household use.
choices: It was likely brought from elsewhere, since none appears in the settlement.
It was likely used in homes for food before being placed in graves.
It was likely prized above every other kind of pottery the community made.
It was likely made from local clay specifically for use in burials.
explanation: You need two separate facts. The clay is the same riverbank clay as the settlement's pots, so the ware is local. Petrosyan argues it was made for burial. Only this choice keeps both facts.

A.why: You noticed the ware's absence from the settlement and concluded it wasn't local. The clay tests show it was made from the same riverbank clay as the settlement's own pots.

B.why: No food or oil residue was found, and Petrosyan says the ware was not borrowed from household use. This is the view she argues against.

C.why: Pottery made for burial may sound special, but the text never ranks it against the community's other pottery.

stem: Based on the text, what does Ivers suggest about Hanne Bjerke?
stimulus: Records of the Lennart weavers' guild show that, between 1620 and 1680, members were fined whenever inspectors found cloth dyed with logwood, a cheap dye that faded quickly. Hanne Bjerke was the only member never fined, though her account books show steady purchases of logwood throughout those years. Historian Paul Ivers notes that the same books record large purchases of alum, which fixes logwood's color, and suggests that inspectors, who judged cloth by how it held its color, may have been unable to detect logwood in cloth treated this way.
choices: She escaped fines by never selling the logwood-dyed cloth she produced.
She deliberately used alum to deceive the guild's inspectors about her dyes.
She may have sold logwood-dyed cloth that inspectors failed to recognize.
She, like other members, was fined less often after she began buying alum.
explanation: Inspectors judged cloth by whether its color held. Alum fixes logwood's color, and Bjerke bought both. Ivers suggests inspectors 'may have been unable to detect' logwood in her cloth. This choice keeps his hedge ('may') and makes no claim about her intent.

A.why: Ivers's point is that she probably did use logwood and simply wasn't caught. Saying she never sold it reverses his explanation.

B.why: You got the alum insight right and then went further. Ivers says only that inspectors 'may have been unable' to detect the logwood. He says nothing about her intent, and his hedge rules out certainty.

D.why: You described her as part of the group. She was the only member never fined, so she couldn't have been fined 'less often'.

stem: Based on the text, what does Okafor indicate about Hale's 1874 version of the ballad?
stimulus: The ballad "The Miller's Grey Mare" has long been credited to collector Edwin Hale, who printed it in 1874 as a song he had taken down from a Dorset farmhand. However, folklorist Ruth Okafor has located a broadside of the ballad, printed in Bristol in 1852, with nearly identical wording. Okafor does not accuse Hale of inventing his singer. She argues instead that the farmhand probably learned the song from a printed sheet, so that what Hale presented as oral tradition had passed through print first.
choices: It probably came from a real singer whose own source was a printed text.
It was probably copied by Hale himself from the 1852 Bristol broadside.
It shows that most songs Hale collected in Dorset came from printed sheets.
It differs enough from the 1852 broadside to show decades of oral change.
explanation: Okafor accepts that Hale had a real singer. She argues that the farmhand probably learned the song from print. So Hale's version came from a living singer, but the song had passed through print before it reached that singer.

B.why: You found the broadside and jumped to the obvious conclusion, that Hale copied it. Okafor explicitly says she does not accuse Hale. She places the printed source with the farmhand, not with Hale.

C.why: Okafor's argument is about one ballad. Extending it to most of Hale's collection goes beyond what she says.

D.why: The text says the broadside has nearly identical wording, so the two versions don't differ enough to show oral change.

stem: Based on the text, what did the planners conclude about the traffic that Fenn Avenue lost?
stimulus: When the city of Marlow narrowed Fenn Avenue from four lanes to two in 2019, planners expected its traffic to shift onto parallel Corder Street. Counts a year later showed that Fenn carried about a third fewer cars, while Corder carried only slightly more than before. Surveys found that some former Fenn drivers now used the ring road and that others had switched to a bus line added the same year. The planners concluded that much of Fenn's lost traffic had not moved to Corder at all but had gone farther afield or out of cars entirely.
choices: Most of it shifted onto Corder Street, as the planners had predicted.
Much of it vanished because the narrowing led people to make fewer trips.
Most of it moved to the bus line, which was added to absorb Fenn's traffic.
Much of it went to a more distant road or to transit instead of to Corder.
explanation: The last sentence puts the facts together. Much of the lost traffic did not go to Corder. It went 'farther afield', which the surveys identify as the ring road, or 'out of cars', meaning onto the bus line. This choice combines both destinations and keeps the planners' word 'much'.

A.why: This was the planners' expectation before the counts. The counts showed only a slight rise on Corder, and the planners concluded the traffic had not moved there.

B.why: The text gives two places the traffic went: the ring road and the bus. It never says people made fewer trips.

C.why: You noticed the bus line and made it the whole answer. The text says 'some' drivers switched to it, not most, and never says why the bus line was added.
